problems.title: Printing text and calculated results
problems.prompt: This calculation assumes you upload 4 videos a day for 30 days and each video gets 2,500 views. Predict the four lines of output without running the code.
hints: Text inside quotes prints exactly as written. An expression without quotes prints its calculated value.
Estimate the last line first. Is 120 times 2500 in the tens of thousands or the hundreds of thousands?
problems.explain:
Text in quotes prints exactly as written, and an expression without quotes prints its value. `4 * 30` is 120, and multiplying that by 2500 gives 300000.
It is easy to write the last line with commas, like 300,000, or to drop a zero. Python prints large numbers without commas. If you estimate about 300,000 before you run the code, you will notice a wrong number of digits right away.
problems.code:
print("Videos uploaded in a month")
print(4 * 30)
print("Views received in a month")
print(4 * 30 * 2500)

expect.stdout:
Videos uploaded in a month
120
Views received in a month
300000
expect.screen:
Videos uploaded in a month
120
Views received in a month
300000

problems.solution:
print("Videos uploaded in a month")
print(4 * 30)
print("Views received in a month")
print(4 * 30 * 2500)

problems.title: Taking the city and the year out of a string
problems.prompt: Print the first character of `s`, its last character, the city name before the underscore, the year after the underscore, and the whole string reversed, one per line in that order. Use indexing and slicing.
hints: Draw tick marks between the characters, starting at 0. The last character is -1.
The character at the end position of a slice is not included. To go all the way to the end, leave the end empty.
problems.explain: `s[0]` is the first character and `s[-1]` is the last. `s[:5]` covers positions 0 through 4, so it is Seoul, and `s[6:]` runs from position 6 to the end, so it is 2026. `s[::-1]` reads one character at a time from the back, which reverses the string.
problems.solution:
s = "Seoul_2026"
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
print(s[:5])
print(s[6:])
print(s[::-1])

problems.title: Fixing code that prints a name and an age
problems.prompt: This code tries to print a name, its first letter, and an age. It has four mistakes, so it stops with an error. Fix it so that it prints `Kim(K): age 19`. The age is the difference in years and ignores birthdays.
hints: If you write only `int(birth)`, where does the converted value go?
Look at the index of the first letter, the `f` before the quotes, and the place where a string and a number are added.
problems.explain:
You need to store the result of `int(birth)` back in `birth` to get an integer. The first letter is `name[0]`; `name[1]` is the second letter.
To put values inside braces, add `f` before the quotes. Adding an integer to a string with `+` raises a TypeError, so put the calculation inside the f-string too.
problems.code:
name = "Kim"
birth = "2007"
int(birth)
first = name[1]
print("{name}({first}): age "
      + (2026 - birth))
problems.solution:
name = "Kim"
birth = "2007"
birth = int(birth)
first = name[0]
print(f"{name}({first}): age {2026 - birth}")

problems.title: The first two and the last two
problems.prompt: The list of posts is long, so the preview shows only the first two and the last two. Fill in the two blanks. There are always at least four posts, and grading runs the code again with different lists.
hints: A slice with an empty start or end runs from the beginning or to the end. A start position can be negative too.
Both sides of `+` must be lists to join them.
problems.explain:
In the first blank, `posts[:2]` gives items 0 and 1. In the second, `posts[-2:]` gives the items from the second to last to the end. Each is a new list. Joining the two lists with `+` makes the preview, and `posts` stays unchanged.
If you leave out the colon, as in `posts[-2]`, you get a single item instead of a list, and `+` raises a TypeError. If you fix the position, as in `posts[4:]`, the code breaks when the number of posts changes, so count from the end with a negative index.
